findings.category: OWASP A04: Insecure Design — DoS / unbounded buffering
findings.issue: The 64 KB per-line cap is enforced AFTER `URLSession.AsyncBytes.lines` has already accumulated the full line into memory. `bytes.lines` is an AsyncSequence that internally buffers bytes until it sees a newline — if a malicious server sends a single 1 GB line without LF, the iterator will allocate ~1 GB before the very first iteration of the for-loop fires and the size check at line 258 even runs. The cap is therefore decorative, not protective. This directly contradicts Decision 10 §7's stated purpose ('protects against a pathological/oversized response line buffering unboundedly in memory'). Tech-spec line 233 and acceptance criterion at tech-spec line 492 both rely on this cap actually being enforced at the buffering level.

findings.category: OWASP A04: Insecure Design — DoS via unbounded `data:` accumulation
findings.issue: The SSE parser accumulates consecutive `data:` field lines into `dataBuffer` (line 282-289) with no overall size cap, only the per-line cap. A malicious or buggy server can send N consecutive `data:` lines each just under 64 KB without an intervening blank-line dispatch, growing `dataBuffer` linearly without bound (e.g. 1000 such lines = ~64 MB held in memory). The 64 KB per-line cap does not transitively bound the event payload. Anthropic in practice sends each event's data on a single line, but the parser must defend against the wire protocol, not the producer's current habits. This also contradicts Decision 10 §7's intent.
findings.recommendation:
Add a payload cap analogous to the line cap. Suggested constant `maxSSEEventBytes = 1 * 1024 * 1024` (1 MB — generous for any realistic Anthropic frame including future tool-use payloads). Check after each append:
```swift
if dataBuffer.utf8.count > Self.maxSSEEventBytes {
    throw AIProviderError.streamingError("SSE event payload exceeds 1 MB cap")
}
```
If a tighter bound (e.g. 256 KB) is preferred, coordinate with the GraphRAG / InsightSession side. Either way, an explicit constant and explicit throw — not implicit reliance on the producer.

findings.category: OWASP A09: Security Logging — sanitize() coverage gap on early-throw paths
findings.issue: Two `try await` calls in `streamCompletion` execute BEFORE the do/catch sanitization wrapper (line 254): `JSONSerialization.data(withJSONObject: body)` (line 221) and `session.bytes(for: request)` (line 230). If either throws, the error propagates raw to the caller without `sanitize(...)` being applied. In practice this is low-risk because (a) `JSONSerialization` will only throw on non-serializable input which cannot happen for two `String` fields, and (b) `URLError` does not embed request headers in its `userInfo` or `localizedDescription` so the `x-api-key` header value should not surface. However, the task-1 acceptance criterion in tech-spec (line 493) and task description (lines 30, 84) state the invariant absolutely: 'No part of API key string ever appears in any thrown error message, JS-side state, or NSLog output.' Relying on Foundation's internal behavior to uphold an absolute invariant is fragile and unverifiable from the call site.

findings.category: OWASP A02: Cryptographic Failures — `apiKeySnapshot` accessor weakens the leakage invariant
findings.issue: The new `internal var apiKeySnapshot: String?` accessor (line 65) intentionally exposes the in-memory key to sibling models for sanitization purposes. The doc comment correctly warns 'never expose publicly'. However, Swift's `internal` access level is module-wide — every type in the MarkView module can read this property, not just the documented sanitization helpers. There is no compile-time enforcement that the snapshot is only consumed by sanitizers, and a future contributor adding a debug log or telemetry call could trivially leak the key by interpolating `apiKeySnapshot` into a log line. The property name is also misleading: it returns the live key, not a snapshot copy.
findings.recommendation:
Two options, choose one based on how widely the snapshot is needed:
(a) If only one consumer needs it: replace the property with a callback API that takes a string and returns a sanitized string in one step, e.g. `func sanitizing(_ msg: String) -> String { sanitize(msg) }`. Consumers call `client.sanitizing(rawText)` and never see the key. This is the secure pattern.
(b) If multiple consumers genuinely need the raw key for redaction: rename to `apiKeyForRedactionOnly` and add a unit-test (when the test target lands) that greps the production sources for accesses to that name and asserts they are all in files matching `*Sanitiz*` or similar. Document the convention in CLAUDE.md or a security-policy file.
Option (a) is strongly preferred — it removes the foot-gun entirely.

findings.category: OWASP A09: Security Logging — `extractSingleChunk` NSLog raw text
findings.issue: Pre-existing (not introduced by this commit, but in the same file under review): `extractSingleChunk` at line 173 logs `NSLog("[AIProvider] JSON decode error chunk \(index+1): \(error). Raw: \(jsonText.prefix(200))")`. The `error` and `jsonText` payloads come from the LLM response, not the request, so apiKey-leakage is not the concern — but this raw text could include user content from the .md document that triggered the chunk. macOS NSLog persists to the unified log, which may be visible to other users on the system or included in `sysdiagnose` archives. The task-1 invariant only covers API key, so this does not violate task-1 directly, but it is a compliance gap (e.g. GDPR if a user ever processes personal data through the app) and is right next to the new code being shipped.
findings.recommendation: Out of scope for task-1 strictly. Recommend tracking as a follow-up: (1) replace `NSLog` with `os.Logger` and use `.private` interpolation for any user/LLM content, e.g. `logger.warning("chunk \(idx) decode failed: \(error.localizedDescription, privacy: .public), raw: \(rawText, privacy: .private)")`, which redacts the private fields in Console.app and sysdiagnose unless the device is in development mode. (2) Audit the entire AIProviderClient for similar `NSLog` of LLM-derived strings (line 170, 173, 316, 573) and apply the same treatment.

findings.category: OWASP A02: Cryptographic Failures — keychain misnomer (pre-existing, out of task-1 scope)
findings.issue: Pre-existing in the file under review (lines 645-651): `loadKeyFromKeychain` and `saveKeyToKeychain` are NAMED for Keychain but actually call `UserDefaults.standard.string(forKey:)` and `set(_:forKey:)`. The API key is therefore stored in plaintext at `~/Library/Preferences/<bundle-id>.plist`, readable by any process running as the user, included in unencrypted iCloud/Time Machine backups by default, and exposed in `defaults read` output. This is a CRITICAL real-world severity but is not introduced by commit 18c6997 — flagging here only because the security focus on this file mentioned 'API key leakage' explicitly and a reviewer should be aware that the at-rest leakage problem dwarfs the in-memory leakage concerns the task is hardening against.
findings.recommendation: Out of scope for task-1 — do NOT block the merge on this. Open a separate ticket (suggest CRITICAL severity) to migrate to actual Keychain storage via SecItemAdd / SecItemCopyMatching with `kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlockThisDeviceOnly` accessibility, and rename the methods or remove the misleading names. Until that ships, the in-memory sanitization in `streamCompletion` is a valuable but insufficient layer.

summary: Two HIGH-severity DoS findings: (1) the 64 KB SSE-line cap fires AFTER `bytes.lines` has already buffered the full line, so a server sending one giant unterminated line bypasses the cap entirely; (2) `data:` field accumulation across consecutive lines has no overall payload cap, allowing N near-64-KB lines to grow `dataBuffer` without bound. Both contradict Decision 10 §7's stated intent and the corresponding tech-spec acceptance criterion. Three LOW findings on apiKey-leakage robustness: pre-loop `try await` calls bypass the sanitize wrapper, the new `apiKeySnapshot` accessor is internal-scope (module-wide) which weakens the invariant, and pre-existing `NSLog` of raw LLM content sits in the same file. Two pre-existing CRITICAL-real-world but out-of-scope-for-task-1 issues noted (UserDefaults masquerading as Keychain; raw NSLog of LLM-derived strings) — flagged for follow-up, not blocking. Sanitize() coverage on the new error paths is otherwise correct: HTTP body, error event, and generic catch are all wrapped; 64 KB constant string is benign; line-cap and error-event payloads cannot leak key. Cancellation handling, forward-compat ignore of unknown events, SSE comment handling, and `apiKey` empty-vs-nil semantics all check out.
